content: Naphthalene, also referred to as naphthalin, naphthaline, mothball, tar camphor, white tar, or albocarbon, is a crystalline, aromatic, white solid hydrocarbon. It is most commonly recognized as the primary ingredient in mothballs. Naphthalene is volatile and produces a flammable vapor. Its molecular structure consists of two fused benzene rings. It is primarily manufactured from coal tar and is converted into phthalic anhydride, which is used in the production of plastics, dyes, and solvents. Additionally, naphthalene serves as an antiseptic and insecticide, particularly in mothballs. However, p-dichlorobenzene is now often used as a substitute for naphthalene in mothballs. Naphthalene readily sublimates at room temperature. In 1819–1820, at least two chemists identified a white solid with a pungent odor derived from coal tar distillation. In 1821, John Kidd described the properties and production methods of this substance and proposed the name naphthaline, as it was derived from a type of naphtha (a term encompassing volatile, flammable liquid hydrocarbon mixtures, including coal tar). Michael Faraday determined naphthalene's chemical formula in 1826. The structure of two fused benzene rings was proposed by Emil Erlenmeyer in 1866 and confirmed by Carl Graebe three years later. A naphthalene molecule consists of two fused benzene rings, meaning the rings share two or more atoms. This structure classifies naphthalene as a benzenoid polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH). Naphthalene has three resonance structures and two sets of equivalent hydrogens. The alpha positions are at positions 1, 4, 5, and 8, while the beta positions are at positions 2, 3, 6, and 7. Unlike benzene, the carbon-carbon bonds in naphthalene are not of uniform length. X-ray diffraction has confirmed that some bonds are shorter (1.36 Å) while others are longer (1.42 Å), consistent with its resonance structures. Naphthalene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution more readily than benzene, reacting under milder conditions. For example, naphthalene reacts with chlorine to form 1-chloronaphthalene even without a catalyst, whereas benzene requires a catalyst. Similarly, naphthalene can be alkylated using alkenes or alcohols with sulfuric or phosphoric acid as a catalyst. Electrophiles typically attack the alpha position due to the stability of the intermediate resonance structures. However, sulfonation reactions yield a mixture of alpha and beta products, with the ratio depending on reaction conditions. Naphthalene can be hydrogenated under high pressure with metal catalysts to produce 1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene (tetralin), a solvent. Further hydrogenation yields decahydronaphthalene (decalin). Oxidation of naphthalene with chromate, permanganate, or catalytic oxygen produces phthalic acid. Most naphthalene is derived from coal tar, which contains about 10% naphthalene by weight. Industrially, coal tar is distilled to yield an oil containing approximately 50% naphthalene, along with other aromatic compounds. This oil is treated with sodium hydroxide to remove acidic components and sulfuric acid to remove basic components, followed by fractional distillation to isolate naphthalene. The resulting crude naphthalene is about 95% pure, with benzothiophene as the main impurity. Petroleum-derived naphthalene, though less common, is typically purer. For higher purity, crude naphthalene can be recrystallized from various solvents. Trace amounts of naphthalene are naturally produced by magnolias and certain deer species. It has also been identified in Formosan subterranean termites, possibly as a repellent against ants, fungi, and nematodes. Naphthalene is widely used as a household fumigant, such as in mothballs. In sealed containers, naphthalene vapors reach levels toxic to moths and their larvae, which damage textiles. It is also used as a soil fumigant pesticide and in attics to repel animals and insects. Historically, naphthalene was administered orally to livestock to kill parasitic worms. Industrially, naphthalene is primarily used to produce phthalic anhydride, although more phthalic anhydride is now made from o-xylene. Other derivatives include alkyl naphthalene sulfonate surfactants and the insecticide carbaryl. Naphthalene derivatives with electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups are intermediates in synthetic dye production. Hydrogenated naphthalenes, such as tetralin and decalin, are used as low-volatility solvents. Naphthalene vapor can also slow rust formation, as seen in the use of mothballs in toolboxes. Exposure to large amounts of naphthalene in humans can damage or destroy red blood cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. This condition has been observed in children who ingested mothballs or deodorant blocks containing naphthalene. Symptoms include fatigue, loss of appetite, restlessness, and pale skin. High exposure may also cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blood in the urine, and jaundice. Studies by the National Toxicology Program found evidence of carcinogenic activity in male and female rats exposed to naphthalene vapors, with increased incidences of nasal adenomas and neuroblastomas. Female mice showed some evidence of carcinogenic activity, with increased incidences of lung adenomas, while male mice showed no evidence of carcinogenic activity. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies naphthalene as possibly carcinogenic to humans. Acute exposure can cause cataracts in humans and animals, and hemolytic anemia can occur in children and infants after oral or inhalation exposure or maternal exposure during pregnancy. Individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, an inherited condition affecting over 400 million people, are more susceptible to hemolytic anemia from naphthalene exposure, even at lower doses.
